findings.explanation: Both objects set `bucket = var.bucket_name`, a plain string literal, instead of referencing `module.storage.bucket`. Terraform's dependency graph is built from resource references, not shared literal values, so there is no implicit edge from these objects to `module.storage` (module.helmrepo.tf:1). On a first-time apply into an empty project, Terraform is free to schedule the object uploads in parallel with (or before) the bucket creation, causing a 404/`notFound` failure. It happens to work today only because the bucket already exists from a prior apply.
findings.remediation: Reference the module output instead of the raw variable so Terraform infers the dependency: `bucket = module.storage.bucket` in both google_storage_bucket_object.index.tf and google_storage_bucket_object.robots.tf, or add an explicit `depends_on = [module.storage]` to each resource.
findings.title: Bucket objects are not wired to the bucket-creating module, risking apply-order races

findings.explanation: This object is the Helm repository index (`helm repo index`), which is expected to change every time a chart is published. Without an explicit `cache_control`, GCS applies its default caching behaviour for publicly-readable objects (public-read ACLs get ~1 hour of edge/browser caching by default). Consumers running `helm repo update` shortly after a new chart is published can keep resolving the previous index.yaml until the cache expires, silently masking new releases.
findings.remediation: Set an explicit cache_control on the index object so clients always revalidate, e.g. `cache_control = "no-cache, max-age=0"`.
findings.title: Helm index.yaml has no cache_control, so Helm clients can see a stale chart index

findings.explanation: The README's copy-paste usage block passes `project = var.project`, but variables.tf only declares `bucket_name` and `binding` — there is no `project` input. The module itself sources the project from `data.google_project.pike` (module.helmrepo.tf:3, module.helmrepo.tf:10), not a variable. A new consumer following the README verbatim gets an immediate `An argument named "project" is not expected here` validation error.
findings.remediation: Remove the `project` line from the README example (and drop `version = "0.0.2"` if that's also stale), matching the actual two-variable interface shown in example/examplea/module.helmrepo.tf.
findings.title: README usage example references a `project` variable the module doesn't declare

findings.explanation: Root variables.tf types `binding` as `map(any)`, so Terraform performs no compile-time validation of its shape. example/examplea/variables.tf:11-15 declares the same conceptual variable as `object({ binding_members = list(string), binding_role = string })`. Consumers who use the root module directly (not through the example) get no type checking on `binding_members`/`binding_role` and can pass a malformed map that only fails deep inside the child `storage` module.
findings.remediation: Type the root `binding` variable the same way the example does: `object({ binding_members = list(string), binding_role = string })`.
findings.title: Root `binding` variable is weakly typed (map(any)) while the example redeclares it as a strict object

findings.explanation: `log_bucket = ""` is a literal passed straight through to the child storage module. There is no corresponding input variable on this module, so any consumer who wants access logging on the helm-chart bucket has to fork or patch the module rather than set a variable.
findings.remediation: Expose an optional `log_bucket` variable (default `""` to preserve current behaviour) and pass it through instead of hardcoding.
findings.title: log_bucket is hardcoded to empty string with no variable to override it

findings.explanation: There is no terraform{} / required_providers block anywhere in the root module (confirmed by the pre-commit-terraform docs table in README.md, which renders "No requirements." and provider google version "n/a"). Only example/examplea/terraform.tf pins `google = 7.42.0`. Without a constraint on the module itself, nothing declares which google provider versions this module is known to work with, so a caller could pick an incompatible provider version with no warning from Terraform.
findings.remediation: Add a terraform.tf at the root with a required_providers block for `google`, pinned exactly (holden's HLD_TF_022 rejects `>=`/wildcard-style version constraints) and matching the example's `7.42.0` pin. A `# holden:ignore:HLD_TF_004` suppression is needed since this module is consumed only as a child module and never configures its own backend.
findings.title: Root module declares no required_providers version constraint

suggested_policies.rationale: google_storage_bucket_object resources commonly get uploaded with no cache_control or content_type, which is invisible in code review but produces real-world staleness/content-type bugs (as seen in HOLDEN_BP_002 here). holden has existing policies for google_storage_bucket_object covering create_before_destroy (HLD_GCP_380) and CMEK (HLD_GCP_427) but nothing on cache_control, so this is a genuine gap, not a duplicate.
suggested_policies.yaml:
id: HLD_GCP_XXX  # run: holden next-id --cloud GCP
name: GCS bucket objects should set cache_control explicitly
principle: reliability
severity: LOW
rationale: |
  Without an explicit cache_control, GCS applies its own default caching
  behaviour to bucket objects, particularly for publicly-readable objects.
  For any object whose content is expected to change over time (index
  files, configs, manifests), relying on the platform default can cause
  clients to silently read stale data for up to an hour.
remediation: |
  Set cache_control explicitly based on the object's intended freshness,
  e.g.:
    resource "google_storage_bucket_object" "example" {
      name          = "index.yaml"
      bucket        = google_storage_bucket.example.name
      source        = "index.yaml"
      cache_control = "no-cache, max-age=0"
    }
resources:
  google_storage_bucket_object:
    path: cache_control
    not_null: true
